title: The burning demands of France’s teenagers
gist: French student protests that drew over half a million people are being framed as urban violence, while students' concrete demands on dilapidated schools, teacher shortages, Parcoursup and student costs go unaddressed against a backdrop of education budget cuts and 6,877 arrests, 86% of minors.

insights.claim: French students' core demands include an emergency plan to renovate dilapidated school and university buildings, a proper lunch break of at least 1.5 hours, repeal of the Parcoursup admissions algorithm, EUR1 subsidised meals for all, repeal of differentiated tuition fees for non-European students, and a rent freeze.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Concrete, costed demands signal pressure for fiscal spending on education and student welfare in France.
insights.locator: The first is an emergency plan to renovate

insights.claim: The protests began in Mayotte in late August over a school built for 900 pupils that holds 2,300, and spread to mainland high schools by mid-September, with more than 1,000 of France's 3,700 high schools affected and over 200 blocked by 1 October.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Shows the breadth and speed of contagion of a grievance that began in a neglected periphery.
insights.locator: In the overseas French territory of Mayotte

insights.claim: Parcoursup, created in Macron's first term, is described by students as an unexplained 'black box' and a 'social selection machine' that is elitist and discriminatory.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Algorithmic gatekeeping of education is a rising source of political backlash.
insights.locator: Protesters also asked for the repeal of Parcoursup

insights.claim: French students lost some 20 million lesson hours in 2025 to unreplaced teachers, and the government has cut a further 3,256 teaching posts this year, after a decade of education ministry budget cuts.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Chronic public-service austerity is feeding social unrest and political risk in France.
insights.locator: The shortage of teachers is a nationwide epidemic

insights.claim: The draft 2027 French budget raises education spending by only 1.7 per cent, below inflation, so real education resources would fall further.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Signals continued fiscal tightening in France despite unrest; watch budget fights.
insights.locator: a draft 2027 budget that raises education spending by just 1.7 per cent

insights.claim: Parents, workers and unions marched with teenagers because for many families empty fridges and empty classrooms reflect the same gutted public spending, widening the protest beyond school issues.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Cross-class coalitions raise the odds of sustained mobilisation against Macron's fiscal line.

insights.claim: The government labelled the movement 'urban violence' rather than a school protest and sent riot police to school gates; by 9 October the justice ministry counted 6,877 arrests, 86 per cent of them minors.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Heavy-handed policing of minors raises political cost and risk of escalation.
insights.locator: The government, which chose to label the movement

insights.claim: Macron responded by vowing to make 'insurrectionists' pay and inviting students to file complaints on a government platform, which the author reads as dismissal of the underlying demands.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: A weak policy response suggests the protests may persist or recur.

insights.claim: Severe injuries from police munitions, including a fractured jaw, a torn-off hand and a lost eye, are fuelling outrage and shifting coverage toward violence over grievances.
insights.speaker: Diane de Vignemont
insights.so_what: Injury incidents are a driver of protest escalation and reputational damage to the government.
